source_span: the composite PMI unexpectedly hit a 5-year high of 58.4 in September (vs. 55.3 expected). So that played into the narrative of resilient growth, which in turn would enable the Fed to keep hiking rates to deal with inflation.
source_chain: A: composite PMI hits a 5-year high (58.4 vs 55.3 expected), signaling resilient growth despite rising input costs. Therefore B: that removes the case for a Fed cut and raises hike odds (71% October, 37bps priced by year-end). Therefore C: bond selloff follows -- 10yr yield jumps 15.2bps to a post-2007 high of 5.11%, worsened by a weak 5yr auction (JPM 17537/17539: 3.20bp tail, disappointing end-user demand). Therefore D: equities fall despite the strong data because valuations were priced for rate cuts. Counter-argument (JPM 17539): yields are approaching JPM's 5.5% fair value, and similar overshoot episodes have been buying opportunities, but JPM's own near-term stance stays 'tactically cautious' into the Fed. No explicit invalidation level is stated in the DB note itself; JPM's own calendar (17537) marks PCE on Sep 30 as the next major data test.
pulse_chain: A: composite PMI hits a 5-year high (58.4 vs 55.3), repricing the rate path in one session. Therefore B: 10yr yield closes at 5.11% (post-2007 high) and equity valuations built on rate cuts stop working at that level. Therefore C: markets price 37bps of hikes by year-end (71% October) because the activity beat plus the fastest input-cost rise since 2020 removes the disinflation case for a cut. Therefore D: a weak 5yr auction (3.20bp tail, thin real-money demand, attributed JPMorgan) is the mechanical reason the selloff extended. Counter-argument, attributed JPMorgan: yields are nearing its 5.5% fair value and past overshoots have been buying opportunities, but JPM's own near-term equity stance stays cautious into the Fed since 5.11% is still 30bp+ below that anchor. Invalidation: Sep 30 growth/inflation data is the first hard test of whether the PMI surge is real, and JPM's 5.5% is the level that decides overshoot-to-buy vs repricing-to-respect.
why: The pulse reproduces DB's PMI-to-hawkish-repricing-to-selloff-to-equity-pressure chain and JPM's fair-value buy-the-dip counter (with JPM's own cautious near-term caveat and its Sep-30 PCE date) in the same direction with correct attribution; the pulse's own 'auction is the tell' framing is added synthesis built from sourced facts rather than a reversed or misattributed step, and the unsourced 5.16% intraday tick is a decorative number, not a chain step.
